what: Celanese makes chemicals and engineered plastics. Its largest products are acetyl chemicals — acetic acid and derivatives used in paints, adhesives and textiles — and engineered materials: specialty plastics sold to carmakers, medical device makers and industrial customers.
customers: Carmakers and their suppliers, paint and coatings manufacturers, medical device companies, textile producers and a wide range of industrial customers worldwide.
money: Specialty polymers and compounds sold into automotive, medical and industrial applications.
Acetic acid, vinyl acetate and derivatives, a commodity business where cost position decides everything.
moat: In the acetyl chain, Celanese has among the lowest production costs in the world, which in a commodity means it stays profitable at prices that lose money for competitors. In engineered materials, polymers get specified into a customer’s product and qualified for that application, which makes the position durable once won.
risks: Debt of $13.0B against $1.3B of cash is enormous — more than twice the market value — and it dominates the equity entirely.
Last year’s results showed a 12.2% net loss margin, and revenue has declined from $10.9B in 2023 to $9.5B in 2025.
The engineered materials business depends heavily on automotive production, which has been weak.
Chemical industry overcapacity, particularly from China, has compressed prices across the sector.
Eighteen analysts average a $62.56 target against a $47.40 price, a 32% gap reflecting disagreement about the deleveraging.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $794.0M against a $5.2B market value is a 15% yield, and the shares trade at about 6.6 times free cash flow.
At 0.53 times sales and 9.7 times EV/EBITDA, the enterprise is priced cheaply even allowing for the debt.
A low-cost position in the acetyl chain means Celanese remains profitable at prices that hurt competitors.
Engineered materials polymers are qualified into customers’ products, which makes that revenue sticky.
Trailing net income of $262.0M marks a return to profit after the loss-making year.
watch: Net debt relative to EBITDA. With debt at more than twice the market value, the deleveraging pace determines the equity’s value far more than the chemical cycle does.
view: Celanese is a good chemical company with a balance sheet problem, and the two facts need to be held separately. The business has two halves. The acetyl chain is a commodity where the only thing that matters is cost position, and Celanese’s is among the best in the world — which means it stays profitable at prices where competitors lose money. Engineered materials is better: specialty polymers qualified into a customer’s product, which cannot be swapped without requalification.

The problem is $13 billion of debt against a $5.2 billion market value. That debt came largely from a large acquisition made near the top of the cycle, and it arrived just as chemical demand weakened and Chinese overcapacity compressed prices across the industry. Revenue fell from $10.9 billion to $9.5 billion, last year produced a 12.2% net loss margin, and the equity became a thin residual claim on a much larger capital structure.

That structure is why the numbers look strange in both directions. Free cash flow of $794 million against a $5.2 billion market value is a 15% yield, and 0.53 times sales is a distressed-looking multiple for a business of this quality. Both are correct, and both describe leverage rather than cheapness: the enterprise is reasonably valued at 9.7 times EV/EBITDA, and the equity is volatile because it sits behind $13 billion of claims.

So the investment question has very little to do with chemicals and almost everything to do with arithmetic. If free cash flow keeps running near $800 million and goes to debt reduction, the value transferred to shareholders over several years is very large. If automotive production stays weak and Chinese capacity keeps prices down, the deleveraging stalls and the equity stays where it is or worse. Net debt to EBITDA is the only number that matters, and the eighteen analysts at $62.56 are modelling the first path.
bull: Automotive demand recovers while a low-cost acetyl position holds margins, and $800 million of annual free cash flow deleverages $13 billion of debt into a thin equity.
bear: Chinese overcapacity keeps chemical prices down, automotive stays weak, and deleveraging stalls with debt at more than twice the market value.
